title: Troubleshooting and Nonresponse
subtitle: Check measurement, learning, formulation and outcome selection
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating troubleshooting and nonresponse within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain troubleshooting and nonresponse without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in troubleshooting and nonresponse.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to troubleshooting and nonresponse.

sections.explainSimply: When progress stalls, first verify the signal, contingency and goal rather than endlessly changing frequencies.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Nonresponse may reflect artifact, poor reward contingency, fatigue, mismatched target, unrealistic outcomes, comorbidity or a treatment that simply is not effective for this person.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Use predefined review points and stopping rules. Avoid post-hoc explanations that make every result appear to support the protocol.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A medication review: benefit, burden, adverse effects and alternatives must remain visible throughout care.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand troubleshooting and nonresponse to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: More sessions are not automatically the answer.
sections.clinicalPearl: Measure benefit and harm with the same seriousness.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using troubleshooting and nonresponse predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: More sessions are not automatically the answer. Evidence classification: clinical reasoning; no universal algorithm.
